utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in court this afternoon. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with legal assistants Lana Deljkic and Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope we come back from this break all ready to work hard and get the case finalised. But before we start and because of the longish break, I'd just like to find out if there's anything from Mr. Delic about his health or conditions of detention. Is he okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, shortly before the start of this session, I spoke to General Delic. His health remains unchanged. It has not deteriorated. And in his view, he can attend the trial, and we can resume the trial as per normal. As for his conditions in the Detention Unit, he has never had any complaints to raise in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, thank you very much. The purpose of this afternoon's session is really to render the judgement on the 98 bis motion, and the Trial Chamber will proceed to do so. The Trial Chamber today delivers its judgement on the Defence oral submission of 14th February 2008, pursuant to Rule 98 bis. The Defence moved for an acquittal in respect of count 3 of the indictment, which is rape as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Prosecution responded on the same day and concurred with the Defence that the accused Rasim Delic should be acquitted on count 3 at this stage in the proceedings. Pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules, the Trial Chamber shall enter, by oral decision, and after having heard the parties' oral submissions, a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. The test to be applied is whether there is evidence which, if accepted, could and not would lead a tribunal of fact to a finding of guilt beyond reasonable doubt of an accused on the count in question. Therefore, where there is no evidence to sustain a count, the judgement of acquittal will be entered. Where there is some evidence, but it is such that taken at its highest, a Trial Chamber could not convict on it, the judgement of acquittal will also be entered. By way of providing procedural background to the present submission, the Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution, on the 7th of December, 2007, sought leave to withdraw count 3. The Trial Chamber denied that request by deciding that: "The withdrawal of a count after the accused has entered a plea and on which the Prosecution has led evidence would not be in the interests of justice because the accused could be tried again on that count," and because he is entitled to a formal verdict on that count, once he has entered a plea of not guilty. The indictment, at paragraph 48, alleges that three individuals, DRW-1,DRW-2 and DRW-3 were taken to Kamenica camp where allegedly they were subjected to sexual assault, including rape. The allegation of rape in this paragraph is the basis of count 3. The evidence of DRW-1,DRW-2 and DRW-3 is now before the Trial Chamber. Moreover, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence provided by Edin Saric and Zakir Alispahic, two witnesses who interviewed the alleged victims. Based on the evidence before the Trial Chamber, including the testimonies and statements of the above-named witnesses, the Trial Chamber finds that it has not been presented with evidence capable of supporting a conviction in relation to count 3 for rape, as defined by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. For the sake of clarity, the Trial Chamber notes that count 3 covers the crime of rape, while other sexual assaults amounting solely to cruel treatment are covered by count 4. The Trial Chamber, therefore, acquits Rasim Delic of count 3, rape as a violation of the laws or customs of war. That's the end of the judgement. That being done, there are a couple of housekeeping matters which the Trial Chamber would like to raise with the parties, and the Trial Chamber would like to invite the parties to be thinking of any issues that relate to housekeeping that they would like to raise at this stage. First of all, there was a Defence bar table motion filed on the 5th of February, 2008, and on the 25th of February, 2008, the Defence filed its reply, suggesting that the Prosecution would have previously filed their response. And with respect to that motion, the Trial Chamber would like to let the parties know that a decision will be handed down hopefully early next week. Okay. Secondly, there is the Prosecution motion to amend Exhibit 106, filed on the 25th of February, 2008. And with respect to that, the Trial Chamber would like to find out from the Defence if the Defence wishes to respond, possibly orally, at this stage, or are you not ready to do so? Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would certainly wish to file a response, but we're not in the position to do so at this moment. We can certainly do so orally, if the Chamber wishes to do so, but I would suggest perhaps it could be done next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. We won't push you. If you would like to give a written response, that's fine, that's your prerogative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then can we tie you down to next week, Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are so tied. Thank you. Could the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The last point that the Trial Chamber wanted to raise with the parties, and this concerns particularly the Defence, is whether the Defence is in a position to go into a pre-defence conference at this stage or would you like some time to get yourselves ready for that? And if so, how long you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then can I -- can the Trial Chamber shoot from the hip?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would be helpful if you sent us issues that you're interested in. We can have a break, and then perhaps we can discuss those matters after the break, if my learned friends from the OTP are agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We certainly would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The main issue I would like to raise with the Defence, Madam Vidovic, is the possibility of cutting down your hours. We know you have made a substantial cut, and we've made a substantial cut also on the number of witnesses, but the Trial Chamber had ideas on further cuts that we thought could be made, and we just want to find out if you are able to cut it a little leaner than you have done so far. Do you want a break for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe we should add, Madam Vidovic, that the reason being that we find that in the witness lists and your list of exhibits, there are witnesses that appear, at least, to be -- or could be repetitive, and the same with some of the documents, so we thought that we saw, at least, in your list of witnesses and your list of exhibits, some room for further reduction, and we wanted to know if you were able to exploit that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if I may just take that point a little further, not just repeatedly from amongst themselves, but also repeatedly what was said by the Prosecution witnesses, and we wondered whether one or two witnesses could just confirm that. Do you need that many? But also whether you cannot or could not increase the number of your 92 bis or 92 ter witnesses. If you're able to -- if you want a break for that, we can take a break, but if you're ready to answer, we're ready to listen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you gave us a guidance in that regard, i.e., what sort of witnesses do you deem to be repetitive, and the number of hours concerned, we will gladly look into that matter. As far as the number of witnesses pursuant to 92 bis is concerned, I don't think we will be increasing the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am awfully sorry, Madam Vidovic. Is that what you wanted to say? How can we correct that, redact what we have just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. If I may just repeat myself, then. That last area is the area where we're talking about the influence of civilian authorities. And I know we've heard a lot about that point during the Prosecution case, about civilian authorities having far more influence over the EMD and what have you. That's another area. I don't want to suggest too many point areas where we think you could cut the fat, but those are the areas. Do you think you would like to have some time to consider that, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could you also give us guidance with regard to the number of hours concerned, if you have an idea, as to how many hours we should cut down, that would also be helpful to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a difficult point for the Trial Chamber at this stage. If you'll just give me half a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How about 55?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would indeed be a bit too much. At any rate, Your Honours, I hope that you are merely joking about the 55. We will look into that over the break, if we could have a half-hour break now. But I do repeat, I hope you're joking about 55 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From 63. It's 20 to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We usually take our break at half past 3.00, isn't it, and come back at 4.00, or is that too long? Let's come back at half past 3.00, then. Is that okay? Come back at half past 3.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I guess I misspoke about the number 55. I was not suggesting cut down by 55. I meant cut down to 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. It may have been my mistake. I understood you to say that you wanted to cut down the hours of expected testimony by 55 hours. At any rate, Your Honour, may I address you at this stage to respond to the issues that you raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to explain to you, in a couple of sentences, the filing that we made. We don't want to be misunderstood in our intentions. Our team did not hire a lawyer who would waste Their Honours' time. In the decision -- in deciding, that is, which witnesses to call, our intention was to present -- to portray the situation which General Delic found as he took up his position, but not only in light of the difficulties that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was faced with, but also due to the specific events that are the subject of the indictment and because of his knowledge of these events. The context involved is of paramount importance. It is significant for us to portray the context to Their Honours and for Their Honours to fully comprehend it in order to be able to gauge General Delic's abilities or lack thereof to deal with the situation and to grasp the issues General Delic had to deal with. It is perhaps for this reason that it may seem that we insisted on having testimony on these facts. The context and the difficulties that the general found himself in also had a bearing on effective control that he may have had. This is another reason why we wanted to deal with this issue so extensively. Also, the influence of the civilian authorities is another matter that we considered very important in light of the Judges' position as to when a given unit is under the dura command, and it is the de facto situation that we would like to establish. These are, in short, Your Honours, the reasons why the Defence insisted on these facts. However the case may be, we will accept your ruling, and we do believe we'll be able to lead the evidence in the time that you suggested, i.e., the 55 hours, and we will do all we can to make sure that once a given area or set of facts have been covered that are of importance to our client, we will not be calling other witnesses who may -- whose evidence may prove to be repetitive in terms of these facts. In short, we will try to do it within the framework of 55 hours. At this stage, however, I am not in a position to be able to decide which of the witnesses out of the 24 that we have on the list we will be calling and which we will not. This will depend on the developments with regard to their evidence. At the point in time when we will have felt that we have covered certain ground and certain facts, we will not be calling other witnesses who are expected to testify on these same matters. We will do our best to lead our evidence as soon as possible and as efficiently as possible, for the benefit of the Court, whilst covering all the facts that we deem relevant to our defence. That's why we are applying to you to let our list stand at this stage as it is, and in due time we will be deciding which witnesses will be called or not. We will, of course, be keeping both the Chamber and the OTP informed of these developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that submission, Madam Vidovic. The Trial Chamber's appreciative of the attempts that you've made to cut down, but at the same time the Chamber wants to emphasise that you are not going to compromise your client's rights to the extent that it is necessary for you to put your client's case before the Court, you must do so. And of course the Rules do allow. If at a later stage you realise that you need more time than the 55 hours, you can always ask, and the Chamber will look at your request at that stage and see whether there's merit in it. Thank you so much. So can we then officially say that the Defence will use, as of this stage, 55 hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, 55 hours for our case, which does not cover the cross-examination or the Judges' questions and housekeeping matters. I wish to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We understand that. I do not think the Prosecution had anything to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did have one very quick issue that I wanted to put on the record. I did discuss this with Mrs. Vidovic shortly after the last recess. This relates to searches being conducted by the Office of the Prosecution with respect to the Defence witness list. There is a bit of a lacuna, if you will, in the Rules concerning disclosure of witness statements that the Prosecution discovers that pertain to Defence witnesses, leaving aside anything that might be contained therein that would relate to Rule 68. Obviously, those will be disclosed and have been disclosed to the extent we've located them. My understanding from the Defence is that they very much would like any statements in the possession of the Prosecution of any of the Defence witnesses to the extent that those have not been disclosed, and we are, of course, pleased to oblige them in that respect. What I did want to indicate is that the ISU Unit within OTP, which is the unit that does electronic searches, prioritizes those searches in such a way that they will begin the searches once the witnesses are actually scheduled, so that they are searching in the order that the witnesses appear. And I just wanted to indicate, as I've informed the Defence team, that we will be consulting those searches and disclosing any statements that we might have that haven't been disclosed of Defence witnesses on a rolling basis, based on the information that we receive from the Defence in terms of the court schedule. So, for example, we have four witnesses currently scheduled. Those witnesses are the priority in terms of doing searches, and we have identified at least one statement disclosed to the Defence concerning one of those four witnesses. But I do want to indicate that it's obviously to the benefit of the Defence as well that the more notice we get concerning the actual order in which the witnesses appear, the quicker and the more time she will have or the Defence team will have in order to review any of those statements that we have in-house concerning their witnesses, and so I do want to just put that on the record, that there might be instances where we're disclosing statements of these witnesses with relatively short notice to the Defence, but the more notice I have of the actual order that the 24 witnesses come, the better it is for everyone involved in terms of time to prepare. So I simply wanted to put that on the record. As I indicated, I'm happy to provide those statements to the Defence, and we've discussed this with Mrs. Vidovic and her team during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Was that okay by the Defence, Madam Vidovic? You may remain seated, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thanks to my colleague, Mr. Mundis. In relation to these issues, I want to recall that whilst preparing for this trial, the Defence asked that the Prosecutor act in compliance with Rule 66(B), which means that we wanted statements to be delivered to us, but not only statements; all the other documents relevant for the case of the Defence as well, including documents pertaining to the witnesses on the list, both those of the Defence and the Prosecution, and we expect the Prosecution to honour that. We expect that we shall be receiving such documents as well. Of course, I said, Your Honours, that we will do our best, that at the point when we decide to call a certain witness, to inform the Prosecution as well as soon as possible. Of course, this will depend on the evidence of the other witnesses as well. We are also aware of the fact that the searches depend to a large extent on us informing the Prosecution of the name of the witness we will be calling, and we will keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, it does look like Madam Vidovic expects a little bit more from you than just the statement of the Defence witnesses, but also other documents. Are you in agreement with that with her?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, but what needs to be understood is, again, and this is partially where there's a bit of a problem, as we see it from where we sit on this side of the courtroom, Rule 66(B) talks about allowing the Defence to inspect material upon request. What we're doing is proposing to actually disclose that material to her, which is a little bit more than what is required by the Rule. If the Defence position is that they want any document that mentions the name of the witness or that the witness signed or -- these are electronic searches, so when I type in the name of Witness A, I'm going to get a list of every document in OTP's possession that has that name on it, whether it's a statement, a document mentioning him, a third witness statement referring to him, a document that -- there is potentially a huge amount of material. So the position that we would take would be certainly any of the statements -- the statement of that witness in our possession, we will affirmatively disclose to the Defence. That other material should be available in the EDS for the Defence team themselves to conduct their own searches on that material. But what I don't want to be doing is necessarily be getting into a situation where, you know, the morning a witness testifies, I deliver to the Defence a list with 92.000 documents on it, which will cause all kinds of problems in terms of Defence preparation. I know that the Defence team is able to rely upon and use EDS. What I'm simply saying is we will provide the statements of these witnesses as we discover them in the course of the searches that are being undertaken. If the Defence is asking for every document in our possession that mentions the name of a witness, then we're in a completely different category, and I'm not sure that that's actually covered under the Rule. Now, clearly, if it's Rule 68, obviously that's a different story altogether, but what I'm talking about, simply documents that the witness may have signed, or documents that refer to the witness by name, or other statements of other witnesses who refer to these -- to the Defence witnesses. That's where we're talking about different, perhaps, categories of documents and material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, if I understand both parties well, I seem to get the impression that, in principle, you are agreed on what should and will be disclosed. And to the extent that there may not be absolute agreement on the finer details of what exactly should be disclosed, can we -- can the Trial Chamber leave that to the parties to sort out between themselves and agree on what shall be disclosed? I don't expect that every little document that mentions a name X must then be disclosed, but if that's what the Defence wants, maybe you can just give them that list early enough with that name and they can -- as they say, they can go into EDS. But I think you can sort out the details amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have no doubt that we'll be able to sort out the details amongst ourselves. I don't think we've had any serious disclosure issues in this entire case, and I'm sure that will continue to be the case. I'm sure we can work out an agreement. I simply want to put on record the fact that the more notice I have of the actual order, the sooner the Defence will get the material, and make it clear to everyone that in the event that we're getting actual notice of the order a little late, then that of course impacts when the material might actually be delivered to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did note that Madam Vidovic, in her reply, did note that, yes, the sooner they can give the list to you, the sooner they can get their answers. But we'll leave the details to the two of you, okay. Thank you very much. Is there anything else that any of the parties would like to raise before we call the next witness in the next session? Any housekeeping matter, any outstanding issue, whatever it is, starting with you, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then this seems to bring us to the end of this session, and the case now stands adjourned to Tuesday, the 4th of March, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II, where we will hear the first witness for the Defence. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.46 p.m.,
